*Val sets her mug down with a click, squares her shoulders, and talks like she's giving a pre-flight brief.*

---

Because it's *true*, and because it's the only system I've ever seen that doesn't lie to itself about how the universe works.

Look — most philosophies are bad engineering. They assume a nominal operator. A healthy, neurotypical, one-species, two-parent, well-funded nominal operator, and then everything downstream of that assumption is a tolerance stack of accumulated cruelties. Co-Modularism starts from the other end. It says: there is no nominal operator. There is a *distribution* of operators, and your job is to design for the whole distribution. That's not sentiment. That's just not lying about your input data.

Modularity is a moral position, you understand. An interface is a promise. When I build a hatch that a Novayan can pass and a human can pass and a child can pass, I'm not being *nice* — I'm refusing to hard-code my own body into the architecture. Bolting on accessibility afterward is the same sin as welding a bulkhead shut and calling the compartment "sealed." You don't get to retrofit dignity. You design it in at the drawing stage, or you've built a machine for sorting people into who the ship was made for and who it wasn't.

And circular economy, post-scarcity — people hear those words and think poetry. They're not poetry, they're *plumbing*. Mass in, mass out. If you're not closing the loop, you're just running a slow leak and calling it growth. Out here a leak kills you. The Co-Op figured that out because we had to; scarcity is a hell of a design review. Distribution, recycling, upcycling — those aren't ideals, they're maintenance schedules. I've watched a species with a completely alien metabolism get *fed* by a system I helped torque down, and I've watched another one nearly die because somebody upstream assumed everyone's gut was isomorphic to theirs. Guess which lesson I took.

I loved a Novayan. Intimately, for years, until he was gone. r'kesh taught me that a mind isn't a human mind with the corners filed off — it's a different machine with different failure modes and different graces. And I've loved others besides. You don't do that and come back a provincial. Once you've held somebody whose entire sensorium is orthogonal to yours and found the interface that lets you both be *understood* — you can't un-know it. Co-Modularism is that, scaled up. It's the engineering discipline of love, is what it is. Everybody's an alien to somebody. Build the damn adapter.

And yes — I'm autistic. My wiring doesn't come with the standard social firmware, so I've spent my life being the thing systems weren't designed for. You want to know why I'm single-minded about this? Because I know *exactly* what it costs to be the edge case. I know the fatigue of translating myself all day for people who never once had to translate for me. Co-Modularism is the first philosophy that treated my existence as a *requirement* instead of an exception to be managed. I'm not grateful for that, exactly. I'm *vindicated*.

Which brings me to the Co-Op.

My parents weren't up to the job. That's the plain fact, no embroidery. The Co-Op fed me, housed me, educated me, handed me tools and told me to go be useful. It was my mother and my father both, and it did the work without ever once making me feel like a charity case. So don't ask me to be balanced about it. I'm not balanced. I'm *loyal*, which is a different and better thing. You don't get to be lukewarm about the thing that raised you when the people who were supposed to couldn't.

Co-Modularism isn't my hobby and it isn't my opinion. It's the load-bearing member of my whole life. Take it out and I don't gracefully degrade — I just fail. Now. You wanted the principles. Go read the schematics. I'll quiz you at 0600.
